guide.title: Infection Prevention & PPE
guide.lead: Treat every patient's blood and body fluids as infectious, clean your hands constantly, and add PPE for how the germ spreads: contact, droplet or airborne. After an exposure, act within minutes and report it the same shift.

sections.title: Standard precautions: every patient
items: Hand hygiene before and after every contact
Gloves for blood and body fluids
Eye and face protection for splashes, suction and airway work
Gown when clothing may be soiled
Sharps: never recap; straight into a sharps container
Clean and disinfect equipment and the stretcher after each patient

sections.title: Add for the route
rows: MRSA wounds, C. difficile, norovirus, scabies
Surgical mask (and on the patient); eye protection for close airway work
Fit-tested N95 or higher, mask on the patient, maximum ventilation in the ambulance
notes: N95: fit-tested every year and seal-checked every time you put it on.

steps.title: Alcohol rub
steps.text: At least 60% alcohol; rub all surfaces until dry.

steps.title: Soap and water instead
steps.text: When hands are visibly soiled, after C. difficile or norovirus, and after the toilet: at least 20 seconds.

steps.title: On
steps.text: Gown → mask or respirator → eye protection → gloves.

steps.title: Off
steps.text: Gloves → eye protection → gown → mask or respirator (last) → hand hygiene. Clean hands again if they get contaminated at any step.

steps.title: Clean
steps.text: Wash with soap and water; don't scrub, squeeze or use bleach. Flush eyes, nose or mouth with water or saline.

steps.title: Report now
steps.text: To your supervisor, the same shift. Note the source patient.

steps.title: Get assessed
steps.text: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible – ideally within 2 hours, no later than 72 hours. Hepatitis B vaccine or immune globulin if not immune; hepatitis C follow-up testing.

sections.title: Bloodborne viruses
rows: Survives on surfaces up to 7 days. Vaccine – employers must offer it free to at-risk staff (US OSHA).
No vaccine. More than half of infections become chronic; now curable with treatment.
Risk after a needlestick from an HIV-positive source is about 0.3%; PEP lowers it further.

options: Every patient, whatever their infection status
quiz.explanation: Assume all blood and body fluids are infectious.
Also measles, chickenpox and disseminated shingles.

quiz.q: Minimum alcohol content for an effective hand rub:
After a needlestick, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should start:
options: As soon as possible – ideally within 2 hours, no later than 72 hours
Only if the source tests positive
At the end of the week
quiz.explanation: Report immediately so assessment can start.

quiz.q: Which US OSHA standard requires free hepatitis B vaccine for at-risk staff?

options: Wash with soap and water and report to your supervisor now
Report at the end of the shift

quiz.q: Which virus can survive on surfaces for up to 7 days?
options: Hepatitis C only in blood bags

quiz.q: Patient with a productive cough, night sweats and weight loss; you have only gloves. You:
options: Put on an N95, mask the patient, and maximise ventilation
Ask the patient to hold their breath
A patient with an MRSA wound infection
quiz.explanation: Gloves and gown; clean the stretcher afterwards.

quiz.q: Which is true of hepatitis C?
options: No vaccine, and more than half of infections become chronic
It can't survive outside the body

quiz.q: Handwashing with soap and water should last:
Suspected meningococcal disease: your protection is mainly:
options: A surgical mask (droplet precautions), with eye protection for close airway work
quiz.explanation: Unprotected airway exposure needs preventive antibiotics.

flashcards.question: Standard vs transmission-based precautions
flashcards.answer: Standard: every patient. Transmission-based: added for contact, droplet or airborne spread.

flashcards.question: Three transmission-based precautions
flashcards.answer: Contact (gloves, gown), droplet (surgical mask), airborne (fit-tested N95 or higher).

flashcards.question: Soap and water instead of alcohol rub
flashcards.answer: Visibly soiled hands, C. difficile, norovirus, after the toilet.

flashcards.question: Order for removing PPE
flashcards.answer: Gloves → eye protection → gown → mask or respirator last → hand hygiene.

flashcards.question: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis timing
flashcards.answer: As soon as possible – ideally within 2 hours, no later than 72 hours.

flashcards.question: Bloodborne pathogen law (US)
flashcards.answer: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030): exposure plan, PPE, free hepatitis B vaccine, post-exposure care.

flashcards.question: N95 respirator
flashcards.answer: Needed for airborne precautions. Fit-tested every year; seal-check every time you put it on.

critical.scenario: Nursing home: 78-year-old on contact precautions for MRSA in a sacral wound, incontinent, needs full help to move. Your partner goes in with gloves only: 'We're just picking her up.'
critical.question: Best infection-control action?

options.t: Gloves and gown before entering; clean and disinfect the stretcher and ambulance after transport
Gloves only for a quick pickup
Ask staff to clean her first
options.f: Doesn't remove the need for PPE.

critical.explanation: Tell the hospital about the MRSA at handover.
critical.kpi: Applies contact precautions and decontaminates equipment

critical.scenario: In the moving ambulance the patient jerks his arm and a used IV catheter punctures your gloved hand. He injects drugs; hepatitis and HIV status unknown. 15 minutes to hospital.
critical.question: Correct sequence?

options.t: Remove the glove, wash with soap and water (don't squeeze or scrub), tell your partner, report, and get assessed for PEP at the receiving hospital
Finish care and report after the shift

critical.explanation: HIV PEP ideally within 2 hours, no later than 72 hours; hepatitis B protection if not immune.
critical.kpi: Follows post-exposure procedure after a needlestick

critical.scenario: 30-year-old with fever, sore throat, coughing, and a fine rash; others at work are sick. You can't rule out measles. SpO₂ 94%.
critical.question: PPE and infection control?

options.t: N95, eye protection, gloves and gown; surgical mask on the patient; maximum ventilation in the ambulance
Gloves and a surgical mask on you

critical.explanation: Warn the hospital so they can isolate him on arrival.
critical.kpi: Selects airborne precautions for a suspected airborne disease
